## Mountain guides: routes with shifting dates and evolving risks

At the headquarters of the Asociación de Guías de Sierra Nevada, in an austere premises on calle Molinos in Granada, wall calendars are no longer useful for planning the season. Guides now check snow reports with the same frequency they once consulted the almanac, and the dates that for decades set the pace for winter routes have become rough references, useful only as a starting point for a conversation that always ends with the same word: uncertainty.

The circular route of Poqueira, one of the most popular snowshoeing trails on the southern slope, offers a precise example of this temporal shift. Twenty-five years ago, guides scheduled snowshoeing outings well into May, with enough snow at mid-altitudes to complete the ten-kilometer itinerary without stepping on bare rock. Today, that same route becomes impassable for snowshoes in March, and the guides who offer it in their catalogs have had to bring the season forward or replace it with higher-altitude alternatives.

Early thawing not only shortens the season: it transforms the nature of the risk. Snow that disappears ahead of schedule leaves behind an unstable snowpack at higher elevations, where ice plates and spring snow alternate with stretches of loose rock. Veteran guides describe a pattern that repeats each spring with increasing intensity: slab avalanches that trigger without warning on slopes that once remained stable until June, and which now collapse in April with unpredictable consequences.

Statistics from the Guardia Civil confirm what the guides observe on the ground. Rescues related to unstable snow have increased by twenty percent over the last decade, an increase not explained by a higher number of visitors, but by the transformation of snow conditions. Avalanche danger reports issued by the Agencia Estatal de Meteorología increasingly reflect days with considerable risk in spring, precisely when the traditional calendar placed the peak season for crossings.

The association's guides have responded to this scenario with a thorough revision of their protocols. Routes that were once planned weeks in advance are now confirmed with just a forty-eight-hour margin, and alternative itineraries are prepared in triplicate for each outing. A guide who has been working on the southern slope for two decades explains that the mountain no longer allows for any promises: the route that seemed safe on Monday can become a trap on Wednesday, and the client who booked a snowshoeing trek may end up doing a dry hiking route without having changed valleys.

The Federación Andaluza de Montañismo has incorporated this new reality into its training programs. Snow progression courses now include specific modules on reading the snowpack under early thaw conditions, and avalanche rescue drills have been intensified in March and April, when they used to be concentrated in January and February. Instructors insist on an idea that summarizes the paradigm shift: the winter mountain no longer ends when the calendar says it does, but when the snow decides to retreat, and that retreat is becoming increasingly unpredictable.

The economic impact of this temporal shift runs through the entire active tourism chain in the region. Rural accommodations that once filled their rooms in April and May with snowshoeing groups have had to reorient their offerings toward spring hiking, and equipment rental companies have seen demand for snowshoes concentrate into an increasingly shorter period. The guides, for their part, have diversified their proposals: botanical interpretation routes in April, ascents to secondary peaks in May, and a high mountain season that moves forward to June, when it used to begin in July.

Conversations among guides, during rest breaks on the routes, often revolve around the need to communicate this new reality to clients without causing alarm. The visitor arriving in the Alpujarra expecting a classic winter trek must understand that the mountain has changed, that the dates they read in a 2015 guidebook no longer correspond to what they will find, and that flexibility is not an option but a condition for safety. The guides have learned to explain this patiently, aware that the client's trust is as fragile as the snowpack they tread upon.

Data from the Federación Andaluza de Montañismo point to a trend that the guides have already internalized: the snow season is compressing and shifting, but it is not disappearing. Snowshoeing routes remain viable in January and February, and high mountain treks maintain their appeal in the central winter months. What has been lost is predictability, that certainty that allowed an entire season to be planned months in advance and which has now been replaced by constant monitoring of the weather forecast and an adaptive capacity that no training course taught twenty years ago.
